elements.quote: A MedDiet has been associated with improved metabolic syndrome (MetS) outcomes, including a decreased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity, among adults. However, the extent to which different levels of adherence to the MedDiet are associated with MetS outcomes in youth remains poorly understood. Several studies have investigated the associations between adherence to a MedDiet and MetS outcomes among adolescents, 21-26 but the results have been inconsistent.
elements.reason: Summarizes existing adult evidence and prior adolescent studies, and explicitly notes key uncertainties (poorly understood associations and inconsistent findings in youth).

elements.quote: The prevalence of metabolic disorders is increasing globally, especially among adolescents, and this has become a public health concern. To our knowledge, no previous systematic review or meta- analysis has synthesised the available evidence examining the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta- analysis was to investigate whether adherence to a MedDiet is associated with MetS in this population.
elements.reason: Explains the public health importance and the need for this review due to the absence of prior syntheses focused on children/adolescents.
The authors state that no previous systematic review or meta-analysis has synthesized this association in children/adolescents, so explaining overlap with similar reviews does not apply.
This is not a review of intervention effects; eligibility included observational longitudinal and cross-sectional designs only.
A logic model for complex interventions is not applicable because the review synthesizes observational associations rather than complex intervention delivery.

elements.quote: All studies were included in the meta- analysis to assess the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: An explicit objective is stated and reflects a PEO-style framework (Population: children and adolescents; Exposure: adherence to the Mediterranean diet; Outcome: metabolic syndrome). However, it is not presented as a structured question/objective using a named question-formulation framework and lacks full structured detail.

The review synthesizes observational (cross-sectional) studies on associations, not intervention effects; thus PICO comparisons do not apply. Evidence: “A total of eight cross- sectional studies were included in the meta- analysis.” (text_17).

elements.quote: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross- sectional study design.
elements.reason: Specifies key study characteristics for eligibility (population, exposure assessment, outcome, and eligible designs) and broadly states setting (all countries/ethnicities). However, no follow-up requirements are described for longitudinal designs, so not all aspects are fully specified.

elements.quote: we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English.
elements.reason: Language eligibility is reported. The search description also notes studies published before 22 April 2024, but publication/report status (e.g., grey literature, preprints) is not specified, so criteria for report characteristics are incomplete.
No statement distinguishes exclusions due to outcomes not being measured from exclusions due to outcome results not being reported.

elements.quote: However, to narrow the scope of the meta- analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included.
elements.reason: Indicates that the synthesis (meta-analysis) was limited to studies assessing the MedDiet–MetS association, and elsewhere it is stated that eight cross-sectional studies were included. However, specific grouping of studies for each synthesis (e.g., by comparator definitions or measurement tools) and explicit linkage to predefined comparisons are not detailed.

elements.quote: However, to narrow the scope of the meta- analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included.
elements.reason: Provides a rationale for one restriction (limiting the meta-analysis scope). No rationales are given for other notable restrictions (e.g., English language, exclusion of participants with certain diseases, validated questionnaires), so justification is incomplete.

elements.quote: The complete search strategies used for all the databases are presented in online supplemental file 2.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state that the full search strategies for all databases are provided in a supplementary file.

elements.quote: The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024. The search was limited to peer- reviewed studies published in English.
elements.reason: The limits (date coverage, English language, peer-reviewed) are described, but no justification linking these limits to the eligibility criteria is reported in the retrieved text.
No evidence was found that published search approaches/filters were cited or that adaptations were described.
No mention of using natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms was found.
No tools for translating search strings between sources were specified in the retrieved evidence.
There is no description of any validation of the search strategy or validation studies.

elements.quote: A professional librarian was consulted to ensure the quality of the search strategy.
elements.reason: Indicates the search strategy underwent peer input, but the process and any tool used (e.g., PRESS) are not described.
The manuscript does not report whether the search structure was based on PICO or describe an alternative conceptual structure and its development.

elements.quote: meta- analysis included a total of eight studies with a combined sample size of 6562 children and adolescents. The studies were conducted in various countries, such as Spain, 22 Greece, 23 Italy, 24 Iran, 25 26 the USA 27 and Turkey 31 and included cross- sectional studies. However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications.
elements.reason: The characteristics of contributing studies (design, sample size, countries, participant characteristics, exposure/outcome measures) are briefly summarised. elements.quote: These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well- designed systematic review and meta- analysis of paediatric populations.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly interpret their results relative to prior evidence, noting consistency with adult studies and distinguishing their focus from a previous review (Bakaloudi et al.).

elements.quote: However, it should be noted that there was considerable inconsistency among the studies included in our meta- analysis. This variability encompassed differences in study design (cross- sectional vs longitudinal), participant characteristics (eg, age range from early childhood to late adolescence, sample size and geographic region) and tools used to assess adherence to the MedDiet. Some studies have used the KIDMED, a validated instrument specifically developed for children and adolescents, whereas others have employed FFQs and derived MedDiet adherence scores on the basis of predefined criteria. Additionally, definitions of MetS vary across studies, with some applying IDF criteria and others using alternative classifications. These methodological and population differences likely contributed to the observed inconsistency and should be considered when the pooled effect estimates are interpreted.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly describes limitations of the included evidence, including heterogeneity across study designs, populations, adherence assessment tools, and differing definitions of metabolic syndrome, noting how these factors contribute to inconsistency in pooled estimates.

elements.quote: Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. ... Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly identifies review-process limitations, including data conversion for meta-analysis, restricting inclusion to English-language studies, and not conducting a certainty-of-evidence (GRADE) assessment.

While several review-process limitations are listed, the manuscript does not discuss their potential impacts (e.g., how English-only restriction, data conversion, or not performing GRADE might affect the results or conclusions).
